title: The life cycle and the family
subtitle: From brit milah to Kaddish: the covenants of family and home
intro: Jewish life moves in a circle of sacred milestones: the covenant of circumcision, coming of age at the Torah, marriage under the chuppah, peace in the home, the laws of family purity, divorce and, finally, a dignified passing and mourning. This section prepares you to speak about the family with the beit din — precisely, and with respect for every movement.

overview.why: Jewish life moves from covenant to covenant: a child enters the covenant of Avraham, a teenager takes on the duty of the mitzvot, two people stand under the chuppah, the home keeps the peace, and a person's passing is met with dignity and memory. This section is needed so that you understand Judaism as the path of a family, and not as a set of separate rites, and so that you build your own home according to the Torah. Without this it is hard to explain both Shabbat at your own table and why marriage, divorce, and mourning are treated with such care in the Jewish tradition.
overview.examFocus: At the beit din this topic is asked in your own words and about life: why there is brit milah and why the eighth day is not postponed, how a bar mitzvah differs from a celebration, what happens under the chuppah, how you keep shalom bayit, what you will do if a marriage has to be dissolved, and how you will meet mourning. In an Orthodox community, expect a calm question about taharat ha-mishpachah. Prepare an answer in the first person: what this means for your family, and which source stands behind it.
goals: After this section you will be able to explain brit milah: the covenant, the eighth day, and the Jewish name
After this section you will be able to distinguish the age of the commandments from the celebration of bar mitzvah and bat mitzvah
After this section you will be able to describe kiddushin, the ketubah, and the chuppah, and to name the forbidden marriages
After this section you will be able, in your own words, to set out shalom bayit, the mezuzah, and the teaching of children
After this section you will be able to speak about the get, the agunah, shiva, Kaddish, and the basics of family purity

deeper.title: Verses of the Torah about the family
deeper.text: Read in the Tanakh the verses of this section: Bereshit 17:9–14 and 21:4, Vayikra 12:3, Bereshit 2:18 and 2:24, Devarim 6:4–9, Devarim 24:1, Vayikra 18:19. In this way the commandment remains the word of the Torah, and not only a retelling of the lesson.

deeper.title: Ages and an open home
deeper.text: In Pirkei Avot 5:21 there is a scale of ages: five years for Scripture, ten for the Mishnah, thirteen for the commandments. Avot 1:5 adds one sentence about the home: “let your house be wide open.” These are short supports for an answer about the family.

deeper.title: Blessings in the siddur
deeper.text: In the siddur “Vrata Molitvy” (“Gates of Prayer”), find the blessings for brit milah, for an aliyah to the Torah, for kiddushin, for the seven wedding blessings, for immersion, and for Kaddish. Learn the opening lines aloud: a blessing spoken calmly at the beit din persuades more strongly than a retelling.

deeper.title: The life cycle in Telushkin
deeper.text: In Y. Telushkin's “Jewish Literacy,” find the account of brit milah, bar mitzvah and bat mitzvah, the chuppah, divorce, and mourning. It is one continuous retelling: with it you can readily check whether you connect the rites into a single story of a family.

deeper.title: Brit milah and the mezuzah in the Kitzur
deeper.text: The Kitzur Shulchan Aruch, chapters 163 and 164, discusses the eighth day, the mohel, postponement because of health, and pidyon ha-ben; chapter 11 covers where to affix a mezuzah and how to check the scroll. This is practice that an Orthodox beit din may ask about beyond the general meaning.

deeper.title: The mikveh as a spiritual practice in progressive communities
deeper.text: The Reform movement does not regard the laws of niddah as obligatory, but in recent decades many progressive communities have been rediscovering the mikveh as a place of transition: giyur, a wedding, healing, personal milestones. Read this together with the lesson on family purity, so that you see both the classical law and living Reform practice.

lessons.title: Brit milah: the covenant of Avraham
keyIdeas: Brit milah is the sign of G-d's eternal covenant with Avraham (Bereshit 17:11). Avraham circumcised eight-day-old Yitzchak; the commandment overrides the strictness of Shabbat.
Circumcision is on the eighth day (Vayikra 12:3). It is not postponed for the sake of guests; a delay is only because of health. Shabbat and Yom Kippur give way before brit milah.

The mohel acts on the father's behalf and receives the knife from him; the sandak holds the child. Then they wish that he enter the Torah, under the chuppah, and into good deeds, and they hold a seudat mitzvah.

A boy is given his name at the brit milah, a girl in the synagogue. A ger is circumcised before the mikveh; for a man already circumcised, hatafat dam brit is performed. In Reform the procedure depends on the community.

Pidyon ha-ben is the redemption of the firstborn from a kohen on the thirty-first day, for five shekels. Kohanim, Levites, and the son of a kohen's or a Levite's daughter do not perform the redemption.

blocks.text: The covenant of Avraham

Brit milah — “the covenant of circumcision” (Hebrew: *brit* — “covenant,” *milah* — “circumcision”) — is the commandment with which a Jewish boy enters the covenant of Avraham. G-d made this eternal covenant with Avraham when he turned ninety-nine, and commanded him and his descendants: “Every male infant among you shall be circumcised” (Bereshit 17:10). Circumcision itself is the *sign* of the covenant on the body: “Circumcise the flesh of your foreskin — and this shall be a sign of the covenant between Me and you” (Bereshit 17:11). Avraham was circumcised that same day, and he himself circumcised eight-day-old Yitzchak (Bereshit 21:4). The Sages call this commandment one of the greatest: “Great is the mitzvah of circumcision,” teaches Rabbi Yose, “for it overrides the strictness of Shabbat” (Nedarim 31b).

blocks.he: וּנְמַלְתֶּם אֵת בְּשַׂר עָרְלַתְכֶם וְהָיָה לְאוֹת בְּרִית בֵּינִי וּבֵינֵיכֶם
blocks.translit: U-nemaltem et besar orlatchem, ve-hayah le-ot brit beini u-veineichem
blocks.ru: Circumcise the flesh of your foreskin — and this shall be a sign of the covenant between Me and you

blocks.text: Brit milah is performed on the eighth day after birth: “On the eighth day his foreskin shall be circumcised” (Vayikra 12:3). The count follows the Jewish day: an infant born at twilight on Shabbat is circumcised a week later on a weekday, and a baby born on Shabbat is circumcised on the following Shabbat. The eighth day is postponed neither for the sake of guests nor for the sake of a lavish feast; the only delay permitted is for reasons of health, since danger to life overrides any commandment (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 163:4). Shabbat and Yom Kippur, however, give way before brit milah: “Everything required for the circumcision is done on Shabbat” (Mishnah, Shabbat 18:3).
Who performs the circumcision

Brit milah is performed by a *mohel* — a Jew specially trained in the laws and practice of circumcision; a doctor may also be a mohel. According to the Kitzur Shulchan Aruch, the father is obligated to circumcise his son or to appoint a mohel as his emissary: the mohel acts on the father's behalf, so the father hands him the knife and stands beside him (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 163:1). The child is held on the lap by the *sandak* — the rite's honored “sponsor”; it is customary not to appoint the same person as sandak twice for the sons of one father. Tradition gives this role high standing: the sandak is compared to a kohen who brings an offering — hence the care taken in choosing him.
a Jew specially trained in the laws and practice of circumcision; he performs the brit milah

Before the circumcision, blessings are recited. The father, who has entrusted the circumcision to the mohel, speaks of bringing his son into the covenant of Avraham, and the mohel recites the blessing over the commandment itself:

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ עַל הַמִּילָה
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam, asher kidshanu bemitzvotav, vetzivanu al hamilah
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, L-rd, our G-d, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning circumcision
blocks.ref: Kiddushin 29a; Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 163:1; Siddur “Vrata Molitvy” (“Gates of Prayer”)

blocks.text: Right after the circumcision, those present recite a wish that has become familiar in Jewish homes: just as the baby has entered the covenant, so may he enter the Torah, under the chuppah, and into good deeds. In honor of the commandment a meal is held — a *seudat mitzvah*, a commanded meal (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 163:8); and on the night before the brit milah, Ashkenazi communities adopted the warm custom of *shalom zachar*, “peace to the infant”: the family gathers in the newborn's home, reads Torah, and offers refreshments to the neighbors.

blocks.he: כְּשֵׁם שֶׁנִּכְנַס לַבְּרִית כֵּן יִכָּנֵס לְתוֹרָה לְחֻפָּה וּלְמַעֲשִׂים טוֹבִים
blocks.translit: Keshem she-nichnas la-brit, ken yikanes le-Torah, le-chuppah u-le-ma'asim tovim
blocks.ru: As he has entered the covenant, so may he enter the Torah, under the chuppah, and into good deeds
blocks.ref: The prayer formula at a brit milah (Siddur)

blocks.text: A Jewish child's name

At the brit milah a boy is given his Jewish name: the mohel announces it in full — “so-and-so, son of so-and-so.” The custom of naming an infant in honor of ancestors strengthens the bond between generations: Ashkenazi families give a name in memory of a relative who has died, and Sephardi families often in honor of the living. A girl is named in the synagogue: after the birth the father (and, in our days, the new mother herself) is called to the Torah, the blessing “Mi sheberach” is recited — “He who blessed our fathers Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov…” — and the name is announced; in many communities there is a separate joyful rite for this, *simchat bat*, “the joy of a daughter.” In the Jewish tradition a name is not a label, but a mission and a prayer: by it a person is called to the Torah and remembered in the prayers.
Brit milah for a ger

For a man accepting Judaism, brit milah comes before immersion in the mikveh: one who has come to accept Judaism “is circumcised and immersed” (Yevamot 46a). If a man has already been circumcised for medical reasons, a second operation is not required: *hatafat dam brit* is enough — a symbolic drawing of a drop of blood as a sign of the covenant (Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 262:1). A mohel performs this brief act, usually in the mohel's office or at the beit din.

differs.text: In Reform Judaism, brit milah for male gerim has not been regarded as an unconditional requirement of giyur since the era of Classical Reform (the 19th century). Today practice differs: many Reform batei din require brit milah or hatafat dam brit, while certain programs — especially in North America — accept gerim even without circumcision. ROOPI communities in Russia and the CIS, as a rule, require brit milah for men. Be sure to clarify the requirements of the community that is receiving you.

blocks.text: Pidyon ha-ben — redemption of the firstborn

The first son, who “opens the womb” of his mother, was, according to the Torah, designated for service, but in his place G-d took the tribe of Levi; therefore the father is obligated to redeem the firstborn from a kohen by giving him five silver shekels: “From one month of age and upward, redeem them… for silver, five shekels” (Bamidbar 18:16; see also Shemot 13:13–15). This commandment rests on the father — in the same series as circumcising his son and teaching him Torah (Kiddushin 29a). The redemption is performed no earlier than the thirtieth day of life, and on the thirty-first day it is not postponed (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 164:3). Kohanim and Levites, and also the son of a kohen's or a Levite's daughter, do not perform the redemption (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 164:9).

The father brings his son to the kohen together with silver, or with money in the amount of the redemption (about 96 grams of pure silver), declares that this is his mother's firstborn, and recites two blessings: on the commandment of redemption, and “Shehecheyanu.” The kohen asks him: “What do you prefer — the firstborn, or five shekels?” — and, having received the money, blesses the baby with the words “May G-d make you like Efrayim and Menashe” (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 164:4).

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ עַל פִּדְיוֹן הַבֵּן
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam, asher kidshanu bemitzvotav, vetzivanu al pidyon haben
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, L-rd, our G-d, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the redemption of the son

blocks.text: If the father has not redeemed the firstborn, the obligation passes to the beit din and then to the firstborn himself when he grows up: he redeems himself (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 164:8).

Brit milah is the sign of the people's eternal covenant, and not a one-time rite that a new teaching could “rewrite.” The covenant of Avraham is not abolished and is not replaced: it binds together the body, the people, and the Land promised in that same chapter of Bereshit.

cards.front: What does “brit milah” mean?
cards.back: “The covenant of circumcision” — the sign of G-d's eternal covenant with Avraham and his descendants.

cards.front: Where in the Torah is the commandment of brit milah?
cards.back: Bereshit 17:9–14 — the covenant with Avraham; confirmed in Vayikra 12:3.

cards.front: On which day after birth is brit milah performed?
cards.back: On the eighth day (Vayikra 12:3), even if it falls on Shabbat or Yom Kippur.

cards.front: When may the eighth day be postponed?
cards.back: Only because of the child's health: danger to life overrides the commandment (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 163:4).

cards.front: Who is a mohel?
cards.back: A Jew specially trained in the laws and practice of circumcision; he acts on the father's behalf.

cards.front: Who is a sandak?
cards.back: An honored guest who holds the child on his lap during the brit milah.

cards.front: What blessing does the mohel say before the circumcision?
cards.back: “Asher kidshanu be-mitzvotav ve-tzivanu al ha-milah” — over the commandment of circumcision itself.

cards.front: When is a child given a Jewish name?
cards.back: A boy — at the brit milah; a girl — at the naming in the synagogue (the rite of “simchat bat”).

cards.front: What is the full form of a Jewish name?
cards.back: “Name ben/bat (son/daughter) + the father's name”; for a ger after giyur — “ben Avraham ve-Sarah.”

cards.front: What is hatafat dam brit?
cards.back: A symbolic drawing of a drop of blood — a sign of the covenant for a ger who is already circumcised (Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 262:1).

cards.front: What is pidyon ha-ben?
cards.back: The redemption of the mother's firstborn son from a kohen — a remembrance that the firstborn are given to G-d.

cards.front: When, and for what sum, is pidyon ha-ben performed?
cards.back: On the 31st day of life, for five silver shekels (Bamidbar 18:16; Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 164:3).

cards.front: Who does not perform pidyon ha-ben?
cards.back: Kohanim, Levites, and families in which the mother is the daughter of a kohen or a Levite (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 164:9).

cards.front: Which blessings are said at a pidyon?
cards.back: “Al pidyon ha-ben,” over the commandment of redemption, and “Shehecheyanu” (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 164:4).

cards.front: At what age did Avraham make the covenant of circumcision?
cards.back: At ninety-nine; that same day he circumcised himself (Bereshit 17).

cards.front: Whom did Avraham circumcise on the eighth day?
cards.back: His son Yitzchak: he himself circumcised eight-day-old Yitzchak (Bereshit 21:4).

cards.front: Why does Rabbi Yose call circumcision a great mitzvah?
cards.back: Because it overrides the strictness of Shabbat (Nedarim 31b).

cards.front: A baby was born on Shabbat. When is the brit milah?
cards.back: On the next Shabbat: the eighth day is counted by the Jewish day and is not moved.

cards.front: What is the seudat mitzvah at a brit milah?
cards.back: A mitzvah meal in honor of the circumcision (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 163:8).

cards.front: What is shalom zachar?
cards.back: An Ashkenazi custom: on the night before the brit milah the family gathers, reads Torah, and offers refreshments to the neighbors.

cards.front: Who redeems the firstborn if the father has not done so?
cards.back: First the beit din, and when the firstborn grows up — he himself (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 164:8).

lessons.title: Bar mitzvah and bat mitzvah: the age of the commandments
keyIdeas: Bar mitzvah means “son of the commandment,” and bat mitzvah means “daughter of the commandment.” A boy becomes obligated in the mitzvot from the age of 13 years and one day, a girl from 12 years and one day.
Until then the parents answer for the child. From the bar mitzvah the young man puts on tefillin himself and enters a minyan; an Ashkenazi father says “Baruch she-petarani.”
The basis of the ceremony is the aliyah la-Torah and a derashah. The celebration and the meal are a custom, not a commandment: the responsibility begins even without a party.
In Masorti and in Reform a girl reads the Torah and wears a tallit. In Orthodoxy a bat mitzvah is without an aliyah: women are not called to the Torah in a men's minyan.
An adult ger does not need a separate bar mitzvah: the obligation of the mitzvot takes full effect at the moment giyur is completed.

blocks.text: Son and daughter of the commandment

“Bar mitzvah” literally means “son of the commandment,” and “bat mitzvah” means “daughter of the commandment.” It is not a reward and not a diploma, but a natural transition: from a set day a boy or a girl becomes personally responsible for fulfilling the mitzvot. The age is fixed by the Oral Torah. A boy becomes obligated in the commandments from thirteen years and one day, a girl from twelve years and one day, when signs of maturity appear (Mishnah, Niddah 5:6). The day the obligation begins is set by the Jewish calendar — on the date of birth.

blocks.he: בֶּן חָמֵשׁ שָׁנִים לַמִּקְרָא בֶּן עֶשֶׂר שָׁנִים לַמִּשְׁנָה בֶּן שְׁלֹשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה לַמִּצְוֹת
blocks.translit: Ben chamesh shanim la-mikra, ben eser shanim la-mishnah, ben shlosh esreh la-mitzvot
blocks.ru: At five years — to Scripture, at ten — to the Mishnah, at thirteen — to the commandments

blocks.text: What changes on the day of the bar mitzvah

Until coming of age, the parents answer before G-d for the child's conduct. When the bar mitzvah arrives, the young man bears the responsibility himself: the parents do not fulfill the mitzvot for him; he does. By Ashkenazi custom the father says on that day the blessing “Baruch she-petarani” — “Blessed is He who has freed me from punishment on account of this [young person].” From this day the boy himself puts on tefillin and himself keeps all the commandments that rest upon a man; a girl, from her bat mitzvah.

The first practical steps of coming of age are set by custom: a boy is given his own set of tefillin, and in many Ashkenazi communities he begins to put them on about a month before his birthday (by Chabad custom — two months before), so that he can get used to them; Sephardi communities, as a rule, do not do this in advance. From that day the young man becomes part of a minyan, his testimony in religious matters counts in full, and he himself answers for calls to the Torah and for the reading, without his father.

The modern synagogue ceremony is above all an *aliyah la-Torah*, the first call to the Torah: the young man (and, in egalitarian communities, the young woman as well) reads or blesses his or her portion of the weekly parashah and often gives a short talk — a *derashah* — on the meaning of what was read. After the service the family holds a celebration and a kiddush. It is important to remember: the celebration itself and the meal are a good custom of the community, and not a commandment; the commandment is taking on responsibility for the mitzvot, and it begins regardless of any celebration.

Two blessings are said at an aliyah: before the reading — “Blessed is He who chose us from all the peoples and gave us His Torah”; after the reading — thanksgiving for the Torah and for “a good, eternal life.” In these very words a person who has come of age first acknowledges the Torah in public — it is worth learning them ahead of time, and aloud.

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם אֲשֶׁר בָּחַר בָּנוּ מִכָּל הָעַמִּים וְנָתַן לָנוּ אֶת תּוֹרָתוֹ
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam, asher bachar banu mikol ha'amim, ve-natan lanu et Torato
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, L-rd our G-d, King of the universe, who chose us from among all the nations and gave us His Torah

blocks.text: “ascending” — calling a member of the community up to read from the Torah; accompanied by blessings before and after the reading
Bat mitzvah and egalitarian communities

The obligation of mitzvot applies to girls as well — from age twelve, but historically communities marked this more modestly. The first known public bat mitzvah took place in 1922 in New York, when Judith Kaplan, daughter of Mordechai Kaplan, founder of the Reconstructionist movement, read from the Torah on her twelfth birthday. From the 1950s–1960s, a bat mitzvah with an aliyah to the Torah became common practice in Conservative (Masorti) and Reform Judaism: girls read from the Torah, lead the prayer service, and wear a tallit, and some also lay tefillin.

There is an important principle that applies to all movements: exemption from some of the mitzvot does not imply spiritual inequality. Women are exempt from mitzvot tied to a specific time of day or year (Mishnah, Kiddushin 1:7) — this is a legal category, not a judgment of worth. “The promise given to women is greater than the promise given to men — teaches the Talmud. — How did they earn this? By bringing their children to read Torah and directing their husbands to the house of study” (Berachot 17a).

differs.text: In Orthodox communities women are not called up to the Torah in a men's minyan — “for the sake of the community's dignity” (Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 282:3); a bat mitzvah is marked without an aliyah — with a speech, a festive meal, and Torah study — and women do not lay tefillin.

blocks.text: A ger and the “second bar mitzvah”

A person who embraced Judaism as an adult does not “celebrate a bar mitzvah” in the usual sense: the obligation of mitzvot comes upon him in full at the moment his giyur is completed. From that day he is a full member of the people of Israel, and every mitzvah becomes his personal responsibility. In some communities it is customary to warmly mark, a year after his conversion, the first year of full life in the covenant. This, in fact, is the meaning of coming of age in Judaism: not a celebration for celebration's sake, but the readiness to bear independently both the burden and the joy of the mitzvot.

The forms of the celebration — from a modest kiddush to a large family feast — depend on the community and its means; the essence is one: the community publicly takes the young person entering adulthood into its care. There is also a touching custom of the “second bar mitzvah”: at age eighty-three (seventy years of life plus thirteen) a person is called to the Torah again, as if newly entering the age of the mitzvot. For a girl in a traditional family, an important sign of growing up is her own mindful practice: lighting candles, prayer, tzedakah.

Practical advice: learn the order of the aliyah in advance — how to approach, how to hold the pointer, which blessings to recite before and after. The first call to the Torah is one of the most moving moments of entering the community.

cards.front: What does “bar mitzvah” mean?
cards.back: “Son of the commandment” — the onset of personal obligation in the mitzvot for a boy.

cards.front: From what age is a boy obligated in the mitzvot?
cards.back: From thirteen years and one day (Mishnah, Niddah 5:6; Avot 5:21).

cards.front: From what age is a girl obligated in the mitzvot?
cards.back: From twelve years and one day (Mishnah, Niddah 5:6).

cards.front: Where does the Mishnah list the ages of study and mitzvot?
cards.back: Pirkei Avot 5:21: at five — to the Written Torah, at ten — to the Mishnah, at thirteen — to the mitzvot.

cards.front: What does the blessing “Baruch she-petarani” mean?
cards.back: “Blessed is the One who freed me from the punishment due for this (youth)” — a custom of Ashkenazim.

cards.front: What lies at the heart of the synagogue bar mitzvah ceremony?
cards.back: Aliyah la-Torah — the first call to the Torah, reading, and a darshah; the celebration itself is a custom, not a mitzvah.

cards.front: When did the first known public bat mitzvah take place?
cards.back: In 1922: Judith Kaplan read from the Torah in New York.

cards.front: How is bat mitzvah practiced in Masorti and Reform communities?
cards.back: Egalitarian: girls are called to the Torah, read, lead the prayer service, and wear a tallit.

cards.front: How is bat mitzvah marked in Orthodox communities?
cards.back: Without an aliyah to the Torah: a speech, refreshments, and Torah study (Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 282:3).

differs.text: In Orthodox Judaism women are not called up to the Torah in a men's minyan.

cards.front: From which mitzvot are women exempt?
cards.back: From mitzvot tied to a time of day or year (Mishnah, Kiddushin 1:7).

cards.front: What does Berachot 17a say about women's merit?
cards.back: It is greater than men's: women bring their children to learn Torah and direct their husbands to study.

cards.front: Does an adult ger need a “bar mitzvah”?
cards.back: No: the obligation of mitzvot comes upon him in full at the moment his giyur is completed.

cards.front: What does a boy begin to do on his own from bar mitzvah?
cards.back: He lays tefillin and bears personal responsibility for the mitzvot of a man.

cards.front: How is the day of a bar mitzvah determined?
cards.back: By the Jewish calendar — on the birth date, not by the commonly used civil (“passport”) date.

cards.front: When does the Chabad custom begin putting on tefillin before the bar mitzvah?
cards.back: Two months before the Jewish date of the bar mitzvah; in many Ashkenazi communities — about a month before.

cards.front: What happens to a young man's testimony?
cards.back: From bar mitzvah his testimony in religious matters is fully valid, and he answers for himself before the Torah.

cards.front: Which blessing is recited before the reading on an aliyah?
cards.back: “Who chose us from among all the nations and gave us His Torah”.

cards.front: What is a darshah at a bar mitzvah?
cards.back: A short talk on the meaning of the Torah portion he read.

cards.front: When does the “second bar mitzvah” take place?
cards.back: At age eighty-three: seventy years of life plus thirteen; the person is called to the Torah again.

cards.front: How does a girl grow into adulthood in a traditional family?
cards.back: Through mindful practice: lighting candles, prayer, and tzedakah — even without a public aliyah.

cards.front: Is the year after giyur marked?
cards.back: In some communities the first year of full life in the covenant is marked a year after conversion.

lessons.title: Jewish marriage: kiddushin and chuppah
keyIdeas: Marriage is a sacred union, not merely shared housekeeping: “a man shall cleave to his wife” (Bereshit 2:24). Founding a family is the mitzvah of “be fruitful and multiply”.

One does not betroth a woman without seeing her first (Kiddushin 41a). Kiddushin require the groom's own ring and the words “according to the law of Moshe and Israel”; only a divorce can free the wife.
Under the chuppah the nisu'in is completed. The ketubah obligates the husband to support and clothe his wife and guarantees a sum: two hundred zuz for a virgin, one hundred for a widow.
The seven blessings are recited under the chuppah and at the meals of the seven days. The cup is broken in memory of the destruction of the Temple and to temper excessive revelry.
The Torah forbids arayot. Orthodoxy and Masorti do not officiate at intermarriages. Under Orthodox halacha a kohen may not marry a giyoret.

blocks.text: Marriage as a covenant

Judaism sees in marriage not a contract about living together but a sacred union: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and cleave to his wife, and they shall become one flesh” (Bereshit 2:24). G-d Himself, according to the midrash, matches pairs; it is left to a person to accept this gift worthily and keep it. “It is not good for man to be alone” (Bereshit 2:18) — and the sages of the Talmud add: one who lives without a wife has no full joy, no blessing, and no goodness (Yevamot 62b). Founding a family is a mitzvah in itself: the first one said to human beings, still in Eden — “be fruitful and multiply” (Bereshit 1:28).
Shidduch — the search for a spouse

The choice of a spouse is called a *shidduch*. The Talmud sternly warns against hasty decisions: “A man is forbidden to betroth a woman until he has seen her — teaches Rav — lest she later appear repulsive to him” (Kiddushin 41a). Historically parents and matchmakers arranged shidduchs; today young people choose each other themselves, but the wisdom of the community remains: before binding your fate together, get to know each other, ask for advice, and watch how the person treats those close to them and how they relate to the mitzvot. A good question about a future spouse: not “how he carries himself at a celebration,” but “how he carries himself in everyday life, in hardship, and in separation”.
Kiddushin — dedication

A Jewish marriage consists of two acts. The first is *kiddushin* (in antiquity called erusin): the groom gives the bride an item of value — today usually a ring belonging to him personally — pronouncing the words of dedication. Kiddushin are performed under a blessing; from that instant the woman is forbidden to all other men in the world except the groom, and only a divorce can free her. The Mishnah teaches: “A wife is betrothed in three ways: by money, by document, and by cohabitation” (Kiddushin 1:1) — of these three, only the first, the giving of value, lives on in the ritual today.

blocks.he: הֲרֵי אַתְּ מְקֻדֶּשֶׁת לִי בְּטַבַּעַת זוֹ כְּדַת מֹשֶׁה וְיִשְׂרָאֵל
blocks.translit: Harei at mekudeshet li be-taba'at zo, ke-dat Moshe ve-Yisrael
blocks.ru: Behold, you are consecrated to me with this ring according to the law of Moshe and Israel

blocks.text: “sanctification, dedication” — betrothal, which makes the woman forbidden to all men except the groom
Ketubah and chuppah

The second act of the marriage is *nisu'in*, completed under the *chuppah*, the wedding canopy — a symbol of the new shared home. In antiquity up to a year could pass between kiddushin and nisu'in; today both are performed in a single ceremony. The irreplaceable document of a Jewish marriage is the *ketubah*: a contract in Aramaic with two witnesses, in which the husband undertakes to support his wife, clothe her, and not diminish her conjugal rights, and — in case of divorce or his own death — to pay the guaranteed sum. The basic sum was set by the Mishnah: two hundred zuz for a virgin and one hundred for a widow or divorcee (Ketubot 1:2). The ketubah is solemnly read under the chuppah and handed to the wife: the document remains her property and her protection.
The seven blessings and the broken cup

Under the chuppah and at the festive meals of the following seven days — at the *sheva brachot* — the seven wedding blessings are repeated. Their texts are collected in the tractate Ketubot (7b–8a); the endings and the exact order differ slightly among rites, but the essence is stable: they begin with the blessing over wine, then praise the Creator of man and of His image, recall Eden, rejoice at the ingathering of children to Jerusalem, and conclude with words about the sanctification of Israel through chuppah and kiddushin.

items: “Borei pri ha-gafen” — “Creator of the fruit of the vine” (the blessing over wine)
“Asher bara sasson ve-simcha” — “Who created mirth and gladness, groom and bride”
“Asher yatzar et ha-adam be-tzalmo” — “Who formed man in His image”
“Sos tasis ha-kara” — “Rejoice and be glad, O barren one” (Yeshayahu 54:1); it concludes with “Who gladdens Zion with children”
“Same'ach te-samach re'im ha-ahuvim” — “Grant joy to the beloved companions, as You gladdened Your creation in Eden”
“Mekadesh amo Israel al yedei chuppah ve-kiddushin” — “Who sanctifies His people Israel through chuppah and kiddushin”

blocks.text: The ceremony ends with the breaking of a cup. The familiar meaning of this ancient detail is *zecher le-churban*, “in memory of the destruction (of the Temple)”: even at the family's highest hour a Jew does not forget the grief of the people and the hope of return. The Talmud (Berachot 31a) tells how Mar bar Ravina smashed an expensive glass at his son's wedding to temper excessive revelry, and reminds us: in exile one must not “fill one's mouth with laughter”. Some people wrap the shards of the cup in cloth and keep them as a family heirloom.
Forbidden marriages

The Torah sharply delineates the circle of permitted marriages. The main prohibitions are *arayot*, the forbidden degrees of blood kinship: mother, sister, daughter, mother-in-law, and other close female relatives (Vayikra 18:6–18; 20:11–21). Some restrictions are tied to status: a kohen is forbidden to marry a divorcee, a woman who has had forbidden relations, or a woman of impaired priestly status (Vayikra 21:7). A child conceived in a union prohibited by arayot — for example, with a married woman who has not received a get — is called a *mamzer* and, under Orthodox halacha, is restricted in marriage rights (Devarim 23:3). This is precisely why Jewish law is so careful about the purity of lines of marriage and divorce.
A ger and a kohen

Under Orthodox halacha a kohen is forbidden to marry a giyoret: the Oral Torah places her in this respect in the forbidden category, and the priestly restrictions apply to the kohen (Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Issurei Biah 19:11; Shulchan Aruch, Even HaEzer 6:8; the basis is the interpretation of the prophet Yechezkel's prohibition: they may take wives only “from the seed of the house of Israel”, Yechezkel 44:22). A male ger, however, is *permitted* to marry the daughter of a kohen: the marriage is fully valid; only the wife loses the right to eat the sacred terumah (Vayikra 22:12). In Conservative and Reform Judaism the priestly restrictions on the marriages of gerim do not apply: a ger is a full Jew in every respect.

differs.text: In Conservative and Reform Judaism the prohibition on a kohen marrying a ger does not apply: a ger is a full member of the community, and the priestly restrictions do not extend to his or her marriages.
In Reform Judaism the priestly marriage restrictions are not observed at all; the status of kohen does not affect the choice of a spouse.

blocks.text: Mixed marriages

A marriage between a Jew and a non-Jew is not recognized by Orthodox and Conservative Judaism: kiddushin are possible only between two Jews, and these communities do not officiate at weddings of mixed couples. Under the Oral Torah, the status of the children follows the mother. The Reform movement sees it differently: since the 1983 resolution it recognizes as Jews also the children of Jewish fathers, provided they are raised exclusively in Judaism; many Reform rabbis agree to conduct a ceremony for a mixed couple — usually on the condition that the children be raised as Jews — though there is no single mandatory position on this.

differs.text: In Reform communities there is no single mandatory position on rabbinic participation in the weddings of mixed couples: many rabbis in North America conduct such ceremonies (often on condition that the children are raised in Judaism), others decline; communities in the CIS usually do not officiate at weddings of mixed couples but openly welcome such families into community life. Questions of status and ceremony are settled with the officiating rabbi.

blocks.text: To the candidate for giyur: discuss the questions of a future marriage and the status of the children with a rabbi in advance — before the engagement, not after. An honest conversation on the shore safeguards both love and the community.

cards.front: Which verse of the Torah is the classic description of marriage?
cards.back: “A man shall leave his father and his mother and cleave to his wife” (Bereshit 2:24).

cards.back: He has no full joy, no blessing, and no goodness (Yevamot 62b).

cards.back: One may not betroth without seeing her first, lest she later appear repulsive.

cards.back: Two: kiddushin (betrothal) and nisu'in (completion under the chuppah).

cards.back: By money (an item of value), by document, by cohabitation (Mishnah, Kiddushin 1:1).

cards.back: In memory of the destroyed Temple (zecher le-churban); also — moderation in joy (Berachot 31a).

cards.back: Forbidden degrees of kinship: mother, sister, daughter, etc. (Vayikra 18).

cards.back: A child of a forbidden union (e.g., of a woman without a get); restricted in marriage (Devarim 23:3).

cards.back: “Be fruitful and multiply” (Bereshit 1:28): founding a family is a mitzvah in itself.

cards.back: It must belong to the groom personally: with this item of value he consecrates the bride.

cards.front: How long do people wait today between kiddushin and nisu'in?
cards.back: No separate waiting at all: both acts take place in one ceremony. In antiquity the interval could reach a year.

cards.front: In what language is a ketubah written?
cards.back: In Aramaic, with two witnesses. The document remains the wife's property and protection.

cards.front: What is the basic ketubah sum for a widow?
cards.back: One hundred zuz. For a virgin the Mishnah sets two hundred (Ketubot 1:2).

cards.front: Where else are sheva brachot recited, besides the chuppah?
cards.back: At the festive meals throughout the seven days after the wedding.

cards.back: A divorcee, a woman who has had forbidden relations, and a woman of impaired priestly status (Vayikra 21:7).

lessons.title: Shalom bayit and the Jewish home
keyIdeas: Shalom bayit — peace in the home. If husband and wife are worthy, the Shechinah rests between them. A home's blessing comes on account of the wife; love her as yourself and honor her more than yourself.
Peace is not kept by silence: do not raise your voice, do not quarrel in front of children and strangers, safeguard each other's dignity even in a joke, and know how to apologize.
The sages applied the words “a small sanctuary” to the synagogue, and the home inherits the same sanctity on a small scale: Shabbat, kashrut, tzedakah, books, and wide-open doors.
The mezuzah is affixed to the right doorpost of one entering; inside are the “Shema” and “Ve-haya”. Ashkenazim hang it slanted; Sephardim — vertically.
A father teaches his child Torah, a trade, and swimming. A home's example is stronger than a lesson; on Friday children are blessed, and parents are honored by deeds.

blocks.text: Shalom bayit — peace in the home

*Shalom bayit* — “peace in the home” — is a special Jewish value, flowing from the very idea of marriage: when husband and wife are worthy, the Shechinah, the Divine Presence, rests between them (Sotah 17a). Peace is achieved not by silence and not by suppression, but by constant honoring of one another: “A man should always be careful about the honor of his wife — teaches the Talmud — for blessing in his house is found only on account of her” (Bava Metzia 59a). And another sage adds: one who loves his wife as himself, honors her more than himself, and raises his children on the straight path — is worthy of blessing (Yevamot 62b).
A man should always be careful about the honor of his wife, for blessing in a man's house is found only on account of her

In practice, shalom bayit means: do not raise your voice, do not sort out conflicts in front of children and strangers, safeguard a spouse's dignity even in a joke, and know how to hear — not merely to listen. The famous “love your fellow as yourself” begins at home: where people are patient, grateful, and know how to apologize, the very walls become walls of peace rather than walls of siege.
The home as a small Temple

Jewish tradition gives the home an almost Temple-like dignity: “And I will be to them a small sanctuary” (Yechezkel 11:16) — the sages interpreted these words above all of synagogues and study halls (Megillah 29a), and the home of a Jew inherits the same sanctity on a smaller scale. What makes a home a “small Temple”? Candles and kiddush on Friday evening, a kosher kitchen, tzedakah in a shared box, a shelf of Jewish books, kind words at the table. Hospitality is an ancient sign of such a home: “Let your house be wide open” (Pirkei Avot 1:5).
A mezuzah on the doors

On the doorpost of a Jewish home a *mezuzah* has hung since time immemorial — a scroll of parchment in a decorative case. It is a direct mitzvah of the Torah: “And you shall write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates” (Devarim 6:9; repeated in 11:20). Inside the scroll are two passages: “Shema Yisrael” (Devarim 6:4–9) and “Ve-haya im shamoa” (Devarim 11:13–21) — the very essence of Jewish faith. The mezuzah is affixed to the right doorpost from the perspective of one entering: the Ashkenazi custom is slanted (a compromise between the opinion of Rashi — vertical — and that of Rabbeinu Tam); the Sephardi custom is vertical.

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ לִקְבּוֹעַ מְזוּזָה
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu, melech ha'olam, asher kidshanu be-mitzvotav, ve-tzivanu likboa mezuzah
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, L-rd, our G-d, King of the universe, who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to affix a mezuzah

blocks.text: The Kitzur Shulchan Aruch devotes an entire chapter to the mezuzah: it is obligatory for a home of permanent residence, and the parchment, written in a special script, should be checked twice in seven years — opening the case and making sure the text is intact (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 11). On the back of the scroll is written the word שדי (Shaddai) — one of the names of G-d: its letters can also be read as an acronym for “Guardian of the doors of Israel.” Touching the mezuzah and bringing one's fingers to the lips — a gesture by which Jewish children learn love for the mitzvah.
Raising children

Children are the main continuation of the home. A father is obligated to circumcise his son, redeem the firstborn, teach him Torah, a trade, and even swimming — “so that he has a path in life” (Kiddushin 29a). Teaching Torah to children is a daily mitzvah: “Teach them to your children and speak of them, when you sit in your house” (Devarim 6:7). The Mishnah sets an age scale: “At five — to the Written Torah, at ten — to the Mishnah” (Pirkei Avot 5:21), and the book of Mishlei advises: “Train a youth according to his way — and he will not stray from it even in old age” (Mishlei 22:6).

blocks.ru: Teach them to your children and speak of them (the words of the Torah)

blocks.text: Example is stronger than instruction: children absorb Shabbat, kashrut and honesty by seeing them in their parents' home, not only by hearing about them in class. The Talmud praises the mother's role especially: women earned a great promise by bringing children to read the Torah and directing their husbands toward study (Berachot 17a). A beautiful custom of many families is blessing the children on Friday evening, laying hands upon them: daughters with the words “may you be like Sarah, Rivka, Rachel and Leah,” sons — “like Efraim and Menashe.”

The center of the Jewish home is Shabbat: candles, kiddush over wine, three festive meals, zemirot at the table. A home in which Shabbat is truly alive itself teaches Torah better than any book. And the foundation of family hierarchy is the mitzvah “each of you shall revere his mother and his father” (Vayikra 19:3): reverence is expressed in details — not interrupting one's elders, serving them first, rising to greet them, caring for them in illness and old age.
Start small: hang a mezuzah on the front door, light the Shabbat candles, place a siddur on the table. A Jewish home grows out of habits, not out of a one-time feat.

cards.front: What does the verse “ve-shinantam le-vanecha” command?
cards.back: To repeat the words of the Torah constantly to one's children and speak of them at home (Devarim 6:7).

cards.front: What does Mishlei 22:6 advise?
cards.back: “Train a youth according to his way — and he will not stray from it even in old age.”

cards.front: In what does the Talmud see the merit of women (Berachot 17a)?
cards.back: Bringing children to read the Torah and directing their husbands toward the house of study.

cards.front: With what words are children blessed on Friday evening?
cards.back: Girls — “like Sarah, Rivka, Rachel and Leah”; boys — “like Efraim and Menashe.”

cards.front: How does Yevamot 62b say one should treat one's wife?
cards.back: Love her as oneself, honor her more than oneself, and lead the children on a straight path.

cards.front: What does shalom bayit not allow during a quarrel?
cards.back: Raising one's voice, arguing in front of children and strangers, and wounding dignity even in jest.

cards.front: What phrase of Avot 1:5 concerns the doors of the house?
cards.back: “Let your house be wide open” — hospitality is the mark of a home that is a sanctuary.

cards.front: What is written on the back of the mezuzah scroll?
cards.back: The name Shaddai. Its letters can also be read as “Guardian of the doors of Israel.”

cards.front: What gesture is associated with the mezuzah?
cards.back: Touch the mezuzah and bring your fingers to your lips: this is how children learn love for the mitzvah.

cards.front: How many festive meals are there at home on Shabbat?
cards.back: Three. Together with the candles, kiddush and zemirot, they make Shabbat the center of the home.

cards.front: How is honoring one's parents done in practice?
cards.back: Do not interrupt, serve them first, rise to greet them, and care for them in illness and old age (Vayikra 19:3).

lessons.title: Laws of family purity (taharat ha-mishpachah)
keyIdeas: Taharat ha-mishpachah — the laws of ritual purity between spouses. Tum'ah is not dirt and not disease, but a status; the Torah calls: “You shall be holy, for I am holy.”
During the days of niddah there is no intimacy, and in Orthodox practice harchakot apply. Then come seven clean days, and on the evening of the seventh — immersion in the mikveh.
A mikveh is no less than forty se'ah, about 760 liters of living water. Before the tevilah, chatzitzot are removed and the blessing over immersion is said.
In Orthodoxy these laws are obligatory. In Masorti, observance is left to the family's discretion. Reform does not consider them obligatory; there the mikveh is sometimes a voluntary practice.
The woman herself keeps the count, and the husband trusts her order. The details are learned with a mentor, not alone from a book: the customs of Ashkenazim and Sephardim differ.

blocks.text: What is taharat ha-mishpachah

The laws of family purity are one of the most intimate chapters of Jewish life. In this lesson the classical system — which must be understood in every movement — is presented first, and then the positions of Masorti and Reform Judaism. The Reform path is described as a full and serious one, not as a “softer” version of the Orthodox.

*Taharat ha-mishpachah* — “family purity” — is a section of halacha on ritual purity between spouses. It is the most personal part of Jewish law, and by convention it is presented with restraint and respect; yet a candidate for giyur needs to know its foundations — without them it is impossible to understand the structure of a traditional Jewish family. The direct source is the Torah: “To a woman during the time of her impurity you shall not approach” (Vayikra 18:19); the Torah punishes its violation in the severest way (Vayikra 20:18). The Talmudic tractate devoted to these laws is called *Niddah*.

It is important to understand the category right away: *tum'ah* — “impurity” — is not dirt and not disease, but a special ritual status, a reminder of human vulnerability and a call to holiness. The same categories of purity operated around the Temple and sacred food; in the family they have been preserved as a daily practice of holiness. The Torah commands: “You shall be holy, for I am holy” (Vayikra 19:2). The laws of family purity are, in the sages' figurative expression, part of the holiness that a Jewish couple keeps in the most intimate corner of life.
The period of niddah

A woman during menstrual bleeding is called a *niddah*; the Torah speaks of seven days of this status (Vayikra 15:19). During these days the spouses abstain from marital intimacy; in Orthodox practice a system of *harchakot* — “distances” — also applies: the spouses do not sleep together, avoid touching, and even avoid handing objects directly from hand to hand. This is not punishment and not revulsion, but a careful form of respect for the mitzvah: a pause agreed upon before G-d.

After the bleeding ends, the woman begins counting *seven clean days* (Vayikra 15:28): if nothing new appears during them, on the evening of the seventh day she is purified by full immersion in the mikveh. By a widespread custom today, the count of clean days does not begin earlier than the fifth day from the start of the period (the practice of Ashkenazi and Sephardi communities; the details of the calculations are individual and are studied with a teacher). A brief daily morning check marks the transition to the clean days.
The mikveh

*Mikveh* — a pool of “living” water of no less than forty se'ah — about 760 liters (Mishnah, Mikvaot 1:7). Rainwater collected from roofs into a cistern, spring water — a mikveh may be arranged in different ways, but the measure and the “naturalness” of the water are obligatory. On the evening of the seventh clean day the woman prepares: she removes everything that separates the water from the body — jewelry, bandages, nail polish; she loosens her hair and cleanses the whole body. This is the removal of *chatzitzot* — “barriers” between the water and the body. Then comes *tevilah* — full immersion of the entire body under the water.

Before the immersion a blessing is recited, and the woman immerses once — briefly, in complete privacy, under the supervision of only the mikveh attendant. After this the family resumes full married life. Tradition sees a deep meaning in this cycle: separation and reunion; a pause that fills the meeting with freshness. The mikveh itself is compared to a womb from which a person emerges renewed. Generations of Jewish wives have kept this cycle as the heart of home holiness, and today teachers all over the world help families observe these laws with joy, not as a burden.

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ עַל הַטְּבִילָה
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu, melech ha'olam, asher kidshanu be-mitzvotav, ve-tzivanu al ha-tevilah
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, L-rd, our G-d, King of the universe, who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning immersion

blocks.text: The mikveh is a concept broader than family life: immersion also completes giyur, the mikveh is used for immersing new dishes (tevilat kelim) and for personal spiritual milestones. In ancient times washings preceded service in the Temple; today the mikveh remains a place of renewal, open also to men who wish to purify themselves before a holiday or on a personal day.
The positions of the movements

A wedding tradition: the bride immerses in the mikveh on the eve of the wedding, and from that evening the cycle becomes the rhythm of the whole family's life. Families who observe these laws often speak of the surprising power of the pause and the meeting: the postponed reunion, marked by ritual, preserves closeness better than habit. That is why communities for so many centuries invested in mikvaot, attendants and teachers — the infrastructure of quiet holiness.

The category of purity is broader than family law: the system of tum'ah and taharah included washings for service in the Temple, rules after childbirth and in other life situations (tractates Taharot, Niddah, Mikvaot). In the family only its living, daily part has been preserved — and it is precisely that part which survived the destruction of the Temple, transferring holiness from stone walls into the bedroom of the home.
The laws of family purity, in the scope presented, are observed in Orthodox Judaism as obligatory: they are considered mitzvot of the Torah and of the Oral Torah.

differs.text: In Conservative (Masorti) Judaism the laws of family purity formally remain, but observance is left to the family's discretion: the practice is encouraged as a beautiful tradition and a means of family renewal, yet it is not considered a condition of piety. Masorti rabbis teach the mikveh as a spiritual practice by choice; in the 20th–21st centuries Conservative responsa have revisited the very obligatoriness of these laws.

The Reform movement has not considered the system of ritual purity and impurity obligatory for the modern Jew since the 19th century; the laws of niddah are not part of the obligatory practice of Reform communities. In recent decades the mikveh has been reviving in many progressive communities as a spiritual symbol — before a wedding, upon conversion, on personal days — by voluntary choice.

blocks.text: The whole system is run by the woman herself: she observes, counts and resolves questions with her teacher, and the husband trusts this order. It is a rare case when the key to home holiness is entirely in women's hands — and tradition is proud that generations of wives have kept it voluntarily and precisely.

The details of the calculation of days, customs and particular cases (health, childbirth, nursing) differ between Ashkenazi and Sephardi communities. Do not rely on memory and do not study alone from a book: the laws of family purity are learned with an experienced teacher or a rabbi — this itself is an old norm of this mitzvah.

In Reform Judaism the laws of niddah and monthly immersion are not part of the community's obligatory practice. This decision is connected with the movement's general view of ritual purity after the destruction of the Temple and with the principle of informed choice. It does not mean that the body, intimacy, a woman's dignity and the holiness of the home are any less important for Reform Jews. The holiness of marriage is built here through mutual respect, consent, honesty, care for health and the equality of partners, as well as through those rituals which the couple consciously embraces.

Since the end of the 20th century, in many progressive communities the mikveh has been experiencing a new flowering — no longer as an obligatory monthly law, but as a **spiritual spring of transition**. People come to the mikveh before a wedding, on the day of their giyur, after illness or loss, at moments when a new chapter of life begins. There are communities that build open, welcoming mikvaot and create new ceremonies of immersion. The woman or man decides for themselves whether this rhythm will become part of their family. A rabbi may offer study of the topic and guidance, but a Reform beit din, as a rule, does not make observance of niddah a condition of giyur.

A candidate should be able to calmly explain both the classical law (niddah, seven clean days, chatzitzah, immersion) and the practice of their own community. At an Orthodox beit din this topic is obligatory and requires study with a mentor. At a Reform one they are more likely to ask whether you know what these things are, and what place (if any) you want to give the mikveh and the holiness of the body in your family.

lessons.title: Divorce: the get and the agunah
keyIdeas: A Jewish marriage is dissolved only by a get, a “sefer keritut”: the sofer writes the scroll, the husband places it in his wife's hand. The formula: “you are permitted to any man.”
A civil divorce alone is not sufficient by halacha. A wife has the right to demand a get through a beit din if the husband does not support her, humiliates her, or disappears.
An agunah is a woman without a get: a new marriage is forbidden to her, and children from it would be considered mamzerim. The mamzer himself is guilty of nothing.

Against the agunah problem stand testimonies of the husband's death and prenuptial agreements. In Masorti there is the Lieberman clause; in Reform a civil divorce is sufficient, though a get is often advised.
If a person died childless, the Torah speaks of yibum; today chalitzah is obligatory instead. The Reform movement abolished both rites.

blocks.text: How a marriage is dissolved

Judaism joins a man and a woman with complete seriousness — and dissolves with the same seriousness. The Torah calls the divorce document a *sefer keritut* — a “scroll of severance”: “When a man takes a wife and marries her, and she does not find favor in his eyes... he shall write her a scroll of divorce and place it in her hand and send her out of his house” (Devarim 24:1). Let us recall: the ketubah promises the wife a payment and release, “if you find a man more suitable for yourself.” A Jewish marriage is dissolved only by a get — not by rumor, not by living apart, and not by a civil divorce alone.

blocks.he: וְכָתַב לָהּ סֵפֶר כְּרִיתֻת וְנָתַן בְּיָדָהּ
blocks.translit: Ve-chatav lah sefer keritut, ve-natan be-yadah
blocks.ru: And he shall write her a scroll of divorce and place it in her hand

blocks.text: The get is written by a specially trained scribe — a *sofer* — according to all the rules, with two witnesses; the husband solemnly hands the document to his wife in the presence of a beit din. The semantic core of the get is the formula of release: “Behold, you are permitted to any man”; from the moment of delivery the woman is free to enter a new marriage. The delivery must be voluntary: the beit din intervenes only when a party refuses without legal grounds. A woman whose married life has become unbearable — the husband does not support her, humiliates her, disappears — has the right to demand a divorce through a beit din.

blocks.ru: Behold, you are permitted to any man

blocks.text: The get is written in a special script and with exact wording: an error in names, dates or words can render the document invalid. That is why only trained scribes take part in the process, and in the traditional world the procedure is not begun without consultation with an experienced beit din. The handing of the scroll to the wife is performed in the presence of two witnesses — she may accept the get not necessarily in the beit din hall; what matters is proper hand-to-hand delivery.

The consequences of divorce are also regulated: the sum promised in the ketubah is paid, the woman is free to enter a new marriage, but for a kohen she becomes forbidden — “neither a divorced woman nor a defiled one shall he take” (Vayikra 21:7). Documents of divorce under Jewish law are carefully preserved: possible descendants must be certain of the purity of their lineage.
Agunah — the “chained” woman

The main wound of Jewish marriage law is the *agunah*, the “chained” woman: one who has not received a get. This happens if the husband refuses to give a divorce out of revenge or in order to extort, if he has disappeared without a trace (killed without witnesses, a soldier missing in action), or if he is incapacitated. According to halacha she remains a married woman: a new marriage is forbidden to her, and children from it would be *mamzerim* (Devarim 23:3) — a most dire situation. For centuries communities solved the problem through witness evidence of the husband's death; in the 20th–21st centuries prenuptial agreements became widespread (the model of the Rabbinical Council of America), obligating the parties to appear before a beit din in case of divorce — and public pressure on husbands who evade it. Concern for agunot is one of the motives with which the traditional world treats the purity of a get so carefully. The mamzer himself is guilty of nothing: tradition forbids only marriage within the community — it is a tragedy of status, not a verdict on the person, and that is precisely why the law strives so hard to prevent agunah.

Since 1953 the Conservative movement has supplemented the ketubah with the so-called Lieberman clause (named for the scholar Saul Lieberman): the spouses undertake in advance to submit to the decision of a beit din if the marriage breaks down. This clause removes the main threat — extortion with a get — and has become one of the symbols of the Masorti attitude toward the agunah problem.

Since the 19th century the Reform movement has regarded civil divorce as sufficient: a get is not required. Many Reform rabbis, however, recommend arranging a get as well, so as not to create future halachic complications for the children — especially if they wish to marry in a traditional community. This is a caring compromise between modern law and the memory of the unity of the people.

In the State of Israel, the marriage and divorce of Jews are under the authority of the Rabbanut — the religious court system — so questions of recognizing giyur and gittin there have state significance and sometimes lead to sharp public disputes. In the Diaspora Jewish and civil law operate in parallel: the family is free to take both systems into account, and a giyur candidate would do well to learn in advance how his future community resolves these questions.
Yibbum and chalitzah

The Torah knows one more institution: if a man dies childless, his brother is obligated to marry the widow (*yibbum*, Devarim 25:5–6), so that the name of the deceased may not disappear. If the brother refuses, the widow performs *chalitzah* over him — “the removal of the shoe”: she takes the shoe off his foot and spits before him, and the knot is undone (Devarim 25:7–10). In all traditional communities chalitzah, rather than yibbum, is obligatory today; marriage with a brother's widow is permitted only in special circumstances. Knowledge of this institution is needed by genealogists as well: without chalitzah, descendants would remain “chained.”

differs.text: The Reform movement abolished yibbum and chalitzah as not matching the modern sensibility; these questions do not arise in its congregations.

blocks.text: A get and a civil divorce regulate different things: a get dissolves a marriage under Jewish law. If you are undergoing giyur within an existing civil marriage — discuss the questions of the get and the status of the family with a rabbi in advance.

lessons.title: Death, funerals, and mourning
keyIdeas: Death is met with simplicity: “The L-rd gave, and the L-rd has taken.” The dust returns to the earth, the spirit to G-d; after a person remain a good name and good deeds.

The hevra kaddisha washes the body and dresses it in white tachrichim without pockets. Burial is in the earth on the day of death or the next; a delay is for the sake of Shabbat, a festival, and the law.
In Orthodoxy cremation is not permitted. Masorti usually avoids it. In Reform there is no single prohibition: the family often decides together with a rabbi.
Kaddish, in Aramaic, says nothing about death: it is the exaltation of the Name of G-d. For parents it is recited for eleven months.
Mourning proceeds in stages: aninut, shiva — seven days, shloshim — thirty days, and for parents — a year. The yahrzeit is marked with a candle and Kaddish; Yizkor is read four times a year.

blocks.text: The Jewish attitude toward death

Judaism cherishes life as the highest value and therefore meets death with humility and simplicity: not pathos, but dignity. “Naked I came from my mother's womb,” says Iyov after all his losses, “and naked I shall return there; the L-rd gave, and the L-rd has taken; blessed be the name of the L-rd” (Iyov 1:21). “And the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to G-d who gave it” (Kohelet 12:7). Death does not erase a person: the soul lives, the memory of the righteous is a blessing, and a Jew's will is to leave behind a good name and good deeds.
The hevra kaddisha and funerals

Funerals are arranged by the *hevra kaddisha* — the “holy society” of volunteers who for centuries have performed selfless care for the dead (*met mitzvah*): they wash the body (*taharah*), dress it in simple white linen garments without pockets — *tachrichim*: equality in the face of death — and lay it in a wooden coffin. Jewish funerals take place quickly: the ideal is on the day of death or the next; “do not leave the dead unburied even for a single night” (Devarim 21:23; Sanhedrin 46b). Delayed funerals, customary in other cultures, are undesirable in the Jewish tradition; a postponement is permitted for the sake of Shabbat and festivals, the arrival of relatives, or the requirements of the law.

Burial is in the earth, among the ancestors. The Torah's word to man: “For dust you are, and to dust you shall return” (Bereshit 3:19) — the body is tenderly returned to the earth. Therefore in Orthodox Judaism cremation is not permitted: it violates the commandment of burial and contradicts faith in the future resurrection of the dead.

differs.text: Conservative communities have also traditionally avoided cremation as contrary to Jewish law; individual Masorti rabbis permit participation in the burial of ashes under extenuating circumstances — positions differ.

In Reform Judaism there is no single prohibition: many congregations and rabbis view cremation with reserve or disapproval, but a significant share of congregations permits it; the family decides on its own, often together with a rabbi.

blocks.text: Kaddish

The symbol of Jewish mourning is the prayer *Kaddish*, written in the Aramaic language. It contains not a word about death: it is a hymn of the exaltation of G-d and the establishment of His kingdom, recited by those left orphaned. Tradition attributes special power to the Kaddish: it raises the soul of the departed and strengthens the living. A son recites Kaddish for his father or mother for eleven months; during the first week it is said in the house of mourning, then in the synagogue at the daily prayers, and at the grave after the funeral.

blocks.ru: May His great Name be magnified and sanctified

blocks.text: Shiva, shloshim, the year

Mourning unfolds in stages. The first is *aninut*, the day before the funeral, when the closest relatives are occupied only with arranging the burial. Then comes *shiva*, seven days: the family sits on low benches or on the ground (the image of mourners sitting on the earth, Eicha 2:10), does not work, removes leather footwear, wears the garment torn at the funeral (kriah), and receives comforters. The Talmudic source for the seven days: “I will turn your festivals into mourning” (Amos 8:10; Moed Katan 20a). After shiva comes *shloshim*, thirty days: the restrictions ease and work resumes. And for parents a *year* of mourning applies: for twelve months a son or daughter abstains from festivities and entertainments.

items: Shiva — seven days: sitting low, the ban on work, comforters at the door of the home.
Shloshim — thirty days: going out among people and working, but no new clothes and no festivities.
The year (for parents) — twelve months of abstaining from public celebrations.
Yahrzeit — the anniversary of death by the Jewish calendar: a candle, Kaddish, a visit to the grave.

blocks.text: The first meal after returning from the cemetery is the *seudat havra'ah*, the “meal of consolation”: neighbors bring food into the house of mourning — bread, eggs, lentils, symbols of the cycle of life — and a silent gesture of care replaces empty words. Jewish comforting is practical: not “do not cry,” but “I am here”; and after shiva has passed, the mourner is the first to return to the living and the everyday. The Sages observed: the departed does not disappear from the hearts of the loved ones before twelve months — hence the special tenderness toward the first anniversary day (Moed Katan 27b).
Yahrzeit and Yizkor

The anniversary of a death by the Jewish calendar is called *yahrzeit* (from the German Jahrzeit — “year-time”): on this day a candle is lit that burns for twenty-four hours, Kaddish is said, the grave is visited, and many take on additional Torah study in memory of the departed. In the synagogue four times a year — on Yom Kippur, Shemini Atzeret, on the last day of Pesach, and on the last day of Shavuot — *Yizkor* is read, the prayer of remembrance of all the departed, in which relatives are named one by one. “Those who mourn for Jerusalem will merit to see its joy” (Yeshayahu 66:10) — memory of the dead and hope for consolation dwell side by side in the Jewish tradition, as grief and faith.

blocks.ru: May G-d remember the soul (of the departed)...
blocks.ref: Yizkor prayer; Siddur “Vrata molitvy” (Gates of Prayer)

blocks.text: Caring for the dying is also part of these laws: loved ones support the one who is departing, read the Shema with him and, when needed, the prayer of repentance (vidui), and do not leave the room, so as not to leave the person alone in the final hour. At the cemetery a Jew brings no flowers: memory is expressed simply — a small stone placed on the grave, and good deeds done in place of the departed.

To the giyur candidate: your first encounter with Jewish mourning may come at a funeral or in a shiva home even before your giyur is complete. Accompanying the dead and comforting the mourners are mitzvot accessible to everyone; do not be afraid simply to be present and to help with small things — your presence itself is the comfort.

questions.prompt: Who does not perform pidyon ha-ben?

Only the families of rabbis
Families in which the firstborn is a daughter
All firstborn sons since the destruction of the Temple

questions.prompt: Brit milah is postponed if the eighth day falls on Shabbat.
questions.explanation: On the contrary: brit milah overrides the prohibitions of Shabbat. A delay is possible only because of the child's health.

questions.explanation: A mohel is a Jew trained in the laws and practice of brit milah; he acts on behalf of the father.

questions.modelAnswer: From thirteen years and one day (for a girl — twelve), a young person becomes personally responsible for the observance of the mitzvot; the parents no longer answer for his transgressions. He puts on tefillin himself, he is called up to the Torah, he himself watches over the observance of Shabbat and kashrut. For a ger a similar transition takes place at the moment the giyur is completed: from then on every mitzvah is his personal responsibility.

questions.prompt: How do kiddushin differ from civil marriage?
questions.modelAnswer: Kiddushin is an act of dedication: the groom gives the bride an object of value (a ring) with the words “according to the law of Moshe and Israel,” and she becomes forbidden to everyone else (Mishnah, Kiddushin 1:1). The marriage is completed by nissuin under the chuppah and formalized by a ketubah — a contract in which the husband undertakes to support his wife and to pay her a guaranteed sum (200 zuz, Ketubot 1:2). Dissolution is possible only through a get — a scroll handed to the wife.
keyPoints: giving an object of value — a ring

questions.prompt: Which marriages does the Torah forbid, and how do the movements relate to intermarriage?
questions.modelAnswer: The Torah forbids arayot — the forbidden degrees of kinship (Vayikra 18), restricts the marriages of kohanim (Vayikra 21:7), and establishes the status of the mamzer — a child of a forbidden union (Devarim 23:3). Orthodox and Conservative (Masorti) Judaism do not recognize the marriage of a Jew to a non-Jew and will not officiate at mixed marriages. Since its 1983 resolution, the Reform movement recognizes as Jews children of Jewish fathers when they are raised in Judaism; rabbinic participation in ceremonies for mixed couples is a matter for each individual congregation.
keyPoints: arayot — Vayikra 18
restrictions on kohanim
mamzer — Devarim 23:3

questions.prompt: What can you do to make your home a “small Temple”?
questions.modelAnswer: Hang a mezuzah on the door, light candles and make kiddush on Shabbat, keep kosher, give tzedakah, fill the house with Jewish books, and teach your children Torah — “and you shall repeat them to your children” (Devarim 6:7). A home becomes a “small Temple” through habits and the parents' example: children absorb Shabbat and honesty by seeing them in their parents' home.
keyPoints: mezuzah

questions.prompt: The beit din asks: what are the laws of family purity, and how do the different movements relate to them?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a system of laws about the ritual purity of spouses: the period of niddah (Vayikra 15:19), then seven clean days (Vayikra 15:28), and full immersion in a mikveh of forty se'ah of water (Mikvaot 1:7); intimacy is forbidden during the period of niddah — Vayikra 18:19. In Orthodox Judaism observance is obligatory. In Masorti the laws formally remain, but observance is left to the discretion of the family. Since the 19th century, the Reform movement has not considered the system binding, reviving the mikveh as a voluntary spiritual practice.

questions.prompt: What is an agunah, and how do Jewish communities fight this problem?
questions.modelAnswer: Agunah means “chained”: a woman whose husband refuses to give her a get, has disappeared, or is incapacitated; according to halacha she may not remarry, and children of a new union would be considered mamzerim. Historically, communities accepted witness evidence of a husband's death; in the 20th–21st centuries prenuptial agreements spread (the model of the Rabbinical Council of America), obligating the parties to appear before a beit din in the event of divorce, as well as public pressure on those who refuse.

The first day after the funeral

Twelve
Six
All his life

Every Shabbat
Only at the cemetery
Once a year, on yahrzeit

questions.prompt: Describe the Jewish customs of mourning: what happens in the first week after the funeral and during the year?
questions.modelAnswer: Funerals take place quickly — on the day of death or the next day; the body is washed and dressed in simple white garments. Then seven days of shiva: sitting on low stools, no work, torn clothing, comforters at the door, Kaddish. After shiva — thirty days of shloshim, when work resumes but without festivities; for parents a year of restraint applies. The anniversary — yahrzeit — is marked with a candle, Kaddish, and remembrance; four times a year Yizkor is recited.
