questions.prompt: If a son is born into your family, how will you arrange the brit milah, and why will you not turn it into a party for the guests?
questions.modelAnswer: For me, brit milah is the sign of the covenant of Avraham, not a convenient day for a banquet. The Torah appoints the eighth day, and I will not postpone it for the sake of guests: delay is permitted only when there is a danger to the child's health. The obligation rests on the father: he appoints the mohel as his agent, hands him the knife, and stands beside him, while the sandek holds the baby. In that same hour the Jewish name is announced, and we say the wish — as he entered the covenant, so may he enter into Torah, under the chuppah, and into good deeds. If the eighth day falls on Shabbat or Yom Kippur, I remember that brit milah is performed on such a day.
keyPoints: The eighth day is not postponed for guests; delay only for health reasons
The father appoints the mohel as his agent, hands him the knife, and stands beside him; the sandek holds the child
At the brit milah the name is announced and the wish is spoken for Torah, the chuppah, and good deeds
Shabbat and Yom Kippur give way to brit milah
questions.explanation: The beit din listens for whether the candidate distinguishes the covenant from the celebration and knows that the day is not moved for convenience.

questions.prompt: You are accepting Judaism as an adult, and a child may be ahead of you. What does the age of mitzvot mean to you, and how will you prepare your son or daughter for it?
questions.modelAnswer: For me the age of mitzvot is not a celebration but the day when the mitzvot become a personal duty: for a boy this is thirteen years and one day, for a girl — twelve years and one day by the Jewish calendar. Until then the parents answer for the child before G-d, and afterward the person answers for himself: the young man puts on tefillin himself, and responsibility for the aliyah to the Torah is now his, not his father's. I will explain at home that kiddush and a meal are a fine communal custom, while the mitzvah is the very acceptance of the mitzvot, and it takes effect even without a party. How exactly the day is marked depends on the community, but the duty itself does not. For me personally there is no separate bar mitzvah: all responsibility for the mitzvot began at the moment I completed my giyur.
keyPoints: A boy — 13 years and one day, a girl — 12 years and one day, by the Jewish date
Responsibility passes from the parents to the person himself
The celebration is a custom; the mitzvah — accepting the mitzvot — applies even without a party
For an adult ger, the duty begins upon completing the giyur
questions.explanation: The beit din checks whether the candidate confuses the celebration with the mitzvah and understands that an adult's giyur is already his coming of age in the mitzvot.

questions.prompt: Why do you need specifically a Jewish marriage, and not just living together? What is your chuppah like in your mind?
questions.modelAnswer: I need a Jewish marriage because the Torah sees in it not a shared household but a union: a man leaves his father and mother and cleaves to his wife. At the chuppah the groom gives a ring that belongs to him and says: “Behold, you are betrothed to me with this ring according to the law of Moshe and Israel”; from that minute only divorce can release the wife. I want the ketubah to be a protection, not a beautiful piece of paper: in it the husband undertakes to support and clothe his wife and assigns her a guaranteed sum. The seven blessings and the broken glass will bind our joy to the memory of the destroyed Temple. Before the chuppah I will not decide hastily: first one must see the person in everyday life, in hardship, and in how they relate to the mitzvot.
keyPoints: Marriage is a union according to Bereshit 2:24, not just living together
Kiddushin: his own ring and “according to the law of Moshe and Israel”; only divorce can release her
Ketubah — support, clothing, and a guaranteed sum for the wife
Sheva Brachot and the broken glass; a shidduch without haste
questions.explanation: The beit din wants to hear the living meaning of the chuppah in your life, not a list of terms.

questions.prompt: What is shalom bayit to you, and how will you keep peace in the home on an ordinary weekday?
questions.modelAnswer: For me, shalom bayit is not silence at any price, but respect in which the Shekhinah rests between worthy spouses. I remember the words of the Talmud: a man must be attentive to his wife's honor, because blessing in the home comes on her account, and one who loves her as himself but honors her more than himself is worthy of blessing. On a weekday this means not raising one's voice, not sorting out conflicts in front of children or strangers, not wounding dignity even with a joke, and knowing how to apologize. “Love your fellow” begins in my home. I will keep the same peace through deeds: a mezuzah on the doorpost, Shabbat at the table, and blessing the children on Friday evening.
keyPoints: Shalom bayit is consideration, not suppression; the Shekhinah between worthy spouses
The wife's honor and the blessing of the home
Do not raise your voice, do not quarrel in front of the children, know how to apologize
Peace is also upheld by deeds: mezuzah, Shabbat, blessing the children
questions.explanation: The beit din listens for whether the candidate can turn “peace in the home” into concrete behavior rather than a slogan.

questions.prompt: How will the laws of family purity affect your married life, and from whom will you learn the details?
questions.modelAnswer: I understand Taharat HaMishpachah as a mitzvah of holiness, not hygiene: tum'ah is a ritual status, and the Torah says, “You shall be holy, for I am holy.” During the days of niddah we will abstain from intimacy and keep the harchakot — no shared bed, no touching, no handing things directly from hand to hand; this is a pause before G-d, not a punishment. After the bleeding ends, the wife counts seven clean days and on the evening of the seventh immerses in the mikveh, having removed everything that separates the water from the body. The counting and the decision remain in her hands, and the husband trusts this order; I will accept whatever role is mine. We will not learn the details of the day-count, the customs, and special cases alone from a book — we will go through them with an experienced teacher or a rabbi; that is how this mitzvah has been taught for generations.
keyPoints: Tum'ah is a ritual status and a call to holiness, not dirt
Niddah and the harchakot, then seven clean days and tevilah in the mikveh
Before immersion, chatzitzot are removed
The woman keeps the count; the details are learned with a mentor, not alone from a book
questions.explanation: The beit din watches whether the candidate speaks about family purity respectfully, precisely, and as part of his own future life.

differs.text: In Masorti the laws of family purity formally remain, but observance is left to the discretion of the family: the mikveh is a spiritual practice by choice, not a condition of piety.
The Reform movement does not consider the laws of niddah binding; in many communities the mikveh is a voluntary symbol before a wedding, a giyur, or on a personal day.

A Reform beit din rarely makes the laws of niddah a condition of giyur. What is expected is knowledge of the classical system and an honest word about the role the mikveh and the sanctity of the body will play in your family: a monthly practice, immersions at life's milestones, or another well-considered arrangement.

questions.prompt: If the marriage has to be dissolved, what role does the get play for you alongside the civil divorce, and how will you protect the woman from the situation of an agunah?
questions.modelAnswer: Under Jewish law a marriage ends not by moving apart and not by a civil decree alone, but by a get: a sofer writes the scroll, the husband places it in the wife's hand, and the essence of the formula sounds — “behold, you are permitted to any man.” As long as there is no get, the woman remains a wife; that is the agunah, and children of a new union without a get would be considered mamzerim. I do not want to withhold a get out of revenge or for gain. If the marriage becomes unbearable, the path is to the beit din: the wife has the right to demand a divorce when the husband does not provide, humiliates, or disappears. Even before the chuppah I am ready for an agreement that obligates the parties to appear before a beit din, so that the divorce does not get stuck.
keyPoints: According to halacha, a marriage is dissolved by a get, not by a civil divorce alone
The formula: “behold, you are permitted to any man”
Without a get, the wife is an agunah; children from a new union would be considered mamzerim
A get must not be withheld; there is a path through the beit din and a prenuptial agreement
questions.explanation: The beit din checks whether the candidate understands the gravity of a get and does not take divorce lightly.

differs.text: In Reform Judaism a civil divorce is considered sufficient, and a get is not required; many rabbis still advise arranging a get so as not to create halachic difficulties for the children.

questions.prompt: If a close person passes away, how will you arrange the funeral and the days of shiva? What will you do if you are called to comfort someone before your giyur is completed?
questions.modelAnswer: I will turn to the community and to the hevra kadisha: they will wash the body, dress it in simple white garments without pockets, and bury it in the ground as soon as possible, on the day of death or the next. I choose burial in the ground: the Torah says “for dust you are, and to dust you shall return,” while in Orthodox halacha cremation contradicts this mitzvah. For the seven days of shiva I will sit on a low seat, without work, in torn clothing, and receive comforters. If I am called to a house of mourning before my giyur is completed, I will simply be present and help with small things: presence itself is comfort, not the phrase “don't cry.” I understand Kaddish as the magnification of G-d's name, not as a story about death; for parents it is recited for eleven months, and on the yahrzeit a candle is lit.
keyPoints: The hevra kadisha, tahara, tachrichim, and prompt burial in the ground
In Orthodoxy cremation is not permitted; other movements view it differently
Shiva is seven days; comfort means being present and helping, including before giyur
Kaddish magnifies G-d's name; for parents — eleven months, then the yahrzeit
questions.explanation: The beit din looks at whether the candidate is ready to meet death simply, in a Jewish way, and to comfort through deeds rather than empty words.

differs.text: Conservative communities usually avoid cremation; individual Masorti rabbis in mitigating circumstances allow participation in the burial of ashes, and positions vary.
In Reform Judaism there is no single ban on cremation: many regard it with restraint, but some communities permit it, and the family decides together with the rabbi.

questions.prompt: At what age did Avraham make the covenant of circumcision?
options: When he turned ninety-nine years old
On the night that eight-day-old Yitzchak was born
Right after leaving his father's house
In the year his eldest son was born
questions.explanation: G-d made an eternal covenant of circumcision with Avraham when Avraham was ninety-nine years old, and Avraham was circumcised that same day.

questions.prompt: If a boy is born on Shabbat, on which day does his brit milah fall?
options: On the next weekday after the birth
On the following Shabbat, the eighth day
On the ninth day, to get around Shabbat
On the thirtieth day, together with the redemption
questions.explanation: The count of the eighth day follows the Jewish day: one born on Shabbat is circumcised on the following Shabbat, and that day is not postponed.
questions.source: Lesson: Brit Milah: the Covenant of Avraham

questions.prompt: Why does the father hand the knife to the mohel before the circumcision?
options: So the guests can see how sharp the blade is
So the sandak has time to bless the knife
Because the mohel acts as the father's emissary
Because the synagogue keeps the knife after the ceremony
questions.explanation: The father is obligated to circumcise his son or to appoint the mohel as his emissary. That is why he hands over the knife and stands nearby: the mohel acts on his behalf.

questions.prompt: What question does the kohen ask the father at the redemption of the firstborn?
options: “Are you ready to give your son to the tribe of Levi?”
“Will you name the firstborn after a living grandfather?”
“Have you brought a flour offering instead of the silver?”
“Which do you prefer: the firstborn or five sela'im?”
questions.explanation: Having received the redemption silver, the kohen first asks the father which he prefers — the firstborn or five sela'im — and then blesses the child.

questions.prompt: Immediately after the circumcision, the child is wished entry into Torah, the chuppah, and good deeds.
questions.explanation: The customary wish of brit milah: as the boy has entered the covenant, so may he enter into Torah, the chuppah, and good deeds.

questions.prompt: Shalom zachar is a Sephardic custom of gathering at the home of the newborn on the night after the circumcision.
questions.explanation: Shalom zachar is an Ashkenazic custom, and the gathering is on the night before the brit milah: they read Torah and treat the neighbors.
questions.source: Lesson: Brit Milah: the Covenant of Avraham

questions.prompt: Match the participant or custom of the brit milah with its role.
pairs: on bringing the son into the covenant of Avraham
the honored guest holding the infant on his knees
a festive meal in honor of the mitzvah of circumcision
the Ashkenazic gathering on the eve, at night
questions.explanation: The father blesses the entry into the covenant, the sandak holds the child, a festive meal is held in honor of the mitzvah, and on the eve the Ashkenazim have shalom zachar.
questions.source: Lesson: Brit Milah: the Covenant of Avraham

questions.prompt: How many sela'im of silver does the father give the kohen at the redemption of the firstborn?
questions.explanation: The Torah sets the redemption of the firstborn from one month old at five shekalim of silver; the lesson conveys this measure as five sela'im.

questions.prompt: The father never redeemed the firstborn. On whom does this obligation rest when the son grows up?
questions.modelAnswer: If the father did not redeem the firstborn, the obligation does not disappear. According to the Kitzur Shulchan Aruch, it passes first to the beit din, and when the son grows up — to the son himself: he redeems himself. For me this belongs to the same row of the father's duties as circumcision and the teaching of Torah. The first son, who opened the womb, was intended for service, but instead of the firstborn the Almighty took the tribe of Levi. Therefore the redemption from the kohen on the thirty-first day remains a mitzvah even when the father has missed it.
keyPoints: The duty does not lapse if the father did not redeem
First the beit din, then the firstborn himself
The meaning of the redemption: the tribe of Levi was taken instead of the firstborn
The mitzvah stands in the same row as circumcision and the teaching of Torah
questions.explanation: The lesson states directly: a pidyon missed by the father passes to the beit din, and then to the firstborn himself.

questions.prompt: What does the word “bat mitzvah” literally mean?
options: A festive speech by the open scroll
Daughter of the mitzvah and her personal duty
A girl's first immersion in the mikveh
The naming of a girl in the synagogue
questions.explanation: “Bat mitzvah” means “daughter of the mitzvah”: from this threshold the girl herself is responsible for the mitzvot, just as a boy is from his bar mitzvah.
questions.source: Lesson: Bar Mitzvah and Bat Mitzvah: the Age of Mitzvot

questions.prompt: When does a boy begin putting on tefillin according to the Chabad custom?
options: Only after his first aliyah in the synagogue
At ten years old, together with the start of Mishnah study
Two months before his Hebrew birthday
Only on the day of a big family kiddush
questions.explanation: According to the Chabad custom, tefillin are begun two months before the bar mitzvah; in many Ashkenazic communities — about a month in advance, to get used to it. Sephardic communities generally do not do this in advance.
questions.source: Lesson: Bar Mitzvah and Bat Mitzvah: the Age of Mitzvot

questions.prompt: Why does the Shulchan Aruch not call a woman to the Torah in a men's minyan?
options: Because she does not study the Written Torah
Because aliyah is permitted only to kohanim
Because the bat mitzvah comes later
Because they guard the dignity of the community
questions.explanation: The Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 282:3, explains the refusal to call a woman to the Torah in a men's minyan by the dignity of the community. The bat mitzvah is celebrated without an aliyah.

questions.prompt: What does a young man enter with the onset of bar mitzvah?
options: The membership of the community's minyan
The ranks of the kohanim of his community
The circle of those who write a get
The list of sandaks of the city
questions.explanation: From bar mitzvah a young man joins the minyan, his testimony in religious matters carries full weight, and he himself is now responsible for being called to the Torah.
questions.source: Lesson: Bar Mitzvah and Bat Mitzvah: the Age of Mitzvot

questions.prompt: Before the onset of bar mitzvah, the parents are responsible for the child's conduct before the Almighty.
questions.explanation: Until adulthood the parents are responsible for the child before G-d. From bar mitzvah the young man bears responsibility himself.
questions.source: Lesson: Bar Mitzvah and Bat Mitzvah: the Age of Mitzvot

questions.prompt: Exempting women from time-bound mitzvot implies their spiritual inequality.
questions.explanation: The lesson calls this a legal category, not a judgment of worth. The Talmud says that more is promised to women than to men.

questions.prompt: Match each sign of the age of mitzvot with what stands behind it.
pairs: a short talk on the section just read
girls wear it in Masorti and Reform
a sign of a girl's coming of age in a traditional home
questions.explanation: Avot 5:21 sets age ten for Mishnah. The drashah elucidates the reading, and the form of the bat mitzvah depends on the community: tallit in egalitarian communities, candles and tzedakah in a traditional home.
questions.source: Lesson: Bar Mitzvah and Bat Mitzvah: the Age of Mitzvot

questions.prompt: What is the Ashkenazic father's blessing called on the day of the bar mitzvah?
questions.explanation: By the Ashkenazic custom the father says “Baruch she-petarani”: Blessed is He Who has freed me from the punishment for this youth.
questions.source: Lesson: Bar Mitzvah and Bat Mitzvah: the Age of Mitzvot

questions.prompt: You are called to the Torah for the first time. Which blessings do you read before and after the reading, and what do you affirm with them?
questions.modelAnswer: Before the reading I bless Him Who chose us from among all nations and gave us His Torah. After the reading I give thanks for the Torah and for a good, eternal life. With these words an adult publicly affirms the Torah for the first time. I will learn them aloud in advance and go over the procedure: how to approach, how to hold the pointer, and where to stand. For me this calling matters more than the refreshments: the duty of the mitzvot has already arrived, and the aliyah voices it before the community.
keyPoints: Before the reading: chose us and gave the Torah
After: gratitude for the Torah and eternal life
This is a public affirmation of the Torah
The aliyah procedure is prepared in advance
questions.explanation: The lesson cites both blessings of the aliyah and calls them the first public affirmation of the Torah by an adult.

questions.prompt: Which phrase of the Torah says that a person should not remain alone?
options: “A man shall leave his father and his mother”
The words “be fruitful and multiply”
“It is not good for man to be alone”
“He shall cleave to his wife” in Bereshit
questions.explanation: The lesson begins the topic of marriage with the words “It is not good for man to be alone” (Bereshit 2:18): the union is not only a shared household.

questions.prompt: Which of the three modes of kiddushin named by the Mishnah lives on in today's ceremony?
options: Cohabitation before two witnesses
A written document without handing over an object
The bride's vow under the wedding canopy
The transfer of a value, usually one's own ring
questions.explanation: The Mishnah names money, document, and cohabitation. In today's ceremony only the first mode remains: the transfer of a value, usually the groom's ring.

questions.prompt: What basic ketubah amount does the Mishnah assign to a widow?
options: The sum of one hundred zuz
The sum of two hundred zuz
Five silver sela'im
The sum of one thousand zuz
questions.explanation: Mishnah, Ketubot 1:2, sets two hundred zuz for a virgin and one hundred for a widow or divorcee. This sum is written into the ketubah.

questions.prompt: Whose must the ring be with which the groom consecrates the bride?
options: A ring borrowed from a witness to the ceremony
A ring that belongs to the groom personally
A ring from the dowry already given to the bride
A ring bought by the community for all chuppahs
questions.explanation: Kiddushin is performed with the groom's property. In our time this is usually a ring that belongs to him personally.
questions.source: Lesson: Jewish Marriage: Kiddushin and Chuppah

questions.prompt: The first mitzvah spoken to people, back in Eden, is “be fruitful and multiply.”
questions.explanation: The lesson calls the founding of a family a mitzvah in itself: “be fruitful and multiply” (Bereshit 1:28) was said to people already in Eden.

questions.prompt: Under the current order, one must necessarily wait a whole year between kiddushin and nisuin.
questions.explanation: In ancient times up to a year passed between betrothal and nisuin. Today both acts are performed in one ceremony.
questions.source: Lesson: Jewish Marriage: Kiddushin and Chuppah

questions.prompt: Match each stage of the path to the chuppah with its meaning.
pairs: getting to know a person before the engagement
the second act of marriage, under the canopy
questions.explanation: Shidduch is the search and getting acquainted, erusin is the old name for kiddushin, nisuin is completed under the chuppah, and arayot mark the forbidden kin marriages.
questions.source: Lesson: Jewish Marriage: Kiddushin and Chuppah

questions.prompt: What is the remembrance of the Temple's destruction called at the moment when a glass is broken at the wedding?
questions.explanation: The broken glass is a zecher le-churban, a remembrance of the Temple's destruction. The Talmud in Berachot 31a adds another meaning as well: to moderate excessive rejoicing.

questions.prompt: You are a man after giyur, and the bride is a kohen's daughter. What does Orthodox halacha say about this marriage?
questions.modelAnswer: According to Orthodox halacha, I, a male ger, may marry a kohen's daughter: such a marriage is valid. The wife thereby loses the right to eat the sacred terumah, as Vayikra 22:12 states. The restriction in the other direction is different: a kohen may not take a female giyoret as a wife. In Conservative and Reform Judaism the priestly marriage bans on gerim do not apply. I will still ask the rabbi of my community before the engagement.
keyPoints: For a male ger, marriage to a kohen's daughter is valid
The wife loses the right to eat terumah
For a kohen, a female giyoret is forbidden
In Masorti and Reform this ban does not apply
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes the two directions: a ger may marry a kohen's daughter, while for a kohen a female giyoret is forbidden.

differs.text: In Masorti the priestly marriage restrictions on gerim do not apply: a ger is a full member of the community.
In Reform Judaism the status of kohen does not affect the choice of spouse: the priestly marriage restrictions are not observed.

questions.prompt: With what words does Pirkei Avot speak of a home's hospitality?
options: Repeat the words of the Torah to one's children
Teach a youth a trade and swimming
See the blessing of the home in its guests
Keep the home wide open
questions.explanation: The lesson takes hospitality from Pirkei Avot 1:5: “Let your home be wide open.” This is a sign of the home as a small sanctuary.

questions.prompt: Whom, according to Yevamot 62b, must a husband honor more than himself?
options: His own wife
The Shabbat guest at the table
His eldest son
The rabbi of his community
questions.explanation: The Talmud connects blessing with one who loves his wife as himself, honors her more than himself, and guides his children on a straight path.

questions.prompt: Which verse does the lesson call the foundation of honoring parents?
options: The words “be fruitful and multiply”
“Every one shall revere his mother and his father”
“It is not good for man to be alone”
“And you shall write them on the doorposts of your house”
questions.explanation: The lesson sees the foundation of family hierarchy in the mitzvah “every one shall revere his mother and his father” (Vayikra 19:3).

questions.prompt: How often does the Kitzur Shulchan Aruch command checking the mezuzah parchment?
options: Before every Friday evening
Once, when the case is hung up
Twice in the course of seven years
In every leap year
questions.explanation: The Kitzur Shulchan Aruch commands opening the case twice in seven years and checking whether the text of the scroll is intact.

questions.prompt: According to Bava Metzia 59a, a blessing in the home comes about only because of the wife.
questions.explanation: The Talmud teaches being attentive to a wife's honor, because a blessing in a person's home comes about only because of her.

questions.prompt: Shalom bayit is kept like this: one stays silent about any offense and does not ask forgiveness aloud.
questions.explanation: Peace in the home is achieved through honor, not through silence and suppression. The lesson includes the ability to apologize, not to raise one's voice, and not to argue in front of children.
questions.source: Lesson: Shalom Bayit and the Jewish Home

questions.prompt: What Name of the Almighty is written on the back of the mezuzah scroll?
questions.explanation: On the back of the scroll is written שדי — Shaddai. These letters are also read as a short form for “Guardian of the doors of Israel.”

questions.prompt: How does Shabbat gather the family at your table on Friday evening?
questions.modelAnswer: For me Shabbat is the center of the home. On Friday evening we light the candles and make kiddush over wine. At the table we sing zemirot, and during these twenty-four hours three festive meals take place. I bless the children, laying my hands on them: daughters — to be like Sarah, Rivka, Rachel, and Leah; sons — like Ephraim and Menashe. In this way the home itself teaches Torah more powerfully than any bookshelf.
keyPoints: Candles and kiddush over wine
Three festive meals and zemirot
Blessing the children on Friday evening
A living Shabbat teaches more than a book
questions.explanation: The lesson names Shabbat itself as the center of the Jewish home: candles, kiddush, three meals, zemirot, and the blessing of the children.
questions.source: Lesson: Shalom Bayit and the Jewish Home

questions.prompt: To whom did the sages first of all apply Yechezkel's “small sanctuary,” and what then remains for an ordinary home?
questions.modelAnswer: The words “And I will be for them a small sanctuary” the sages in Megillah 29a applied first of all to synagogues and study halls. A Jew's home inherits the same sanctity on a smaller scale. For me that means candles and kiddush on Friday, a kosher kitchen, a shared tzedakah box, a bookshelf, and kind words at the table. I take hospitality from Pirkei Avot: let the home be wide open. It is from these habits that the sanctity of weekdays grows.
keyPoints: Megillah 29a: first synagogues and study halls
The home inherits sanctity on a small scale
Candles, kiddush, kashrut, tzedakah, books
Avot 1:5 — the home wide open
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes the first interpretation of the verse — about synagogues and houses of study — from the sanctity that the home inherits in miniature.

questions.prompt: What is the Talmudic tractate on the laws of niddah called?
options: Tractate Gittin
Tractate Ketubot
Tractate Sotah
Tractate Niddah
questions.explanation: The laws of family purity are devoted the tractate Niddah. The direct prohibition of intimacy the lesson takes from Vayikra 18:19.

questions.prompt: By the widespread custom of Ashkenazim and Sephardim, the count of clean days is not begun before which day?
options: Before the fifth day from the start of the period
Before the third day after it ends
Before the seventh clean evening
Before the thirtieth day of the month
questions.explanation: By the custom widespread in Ashkenazic and Sephardic communities today, the count of seven clean days is not begun earlier than the fifth day from the start of the period. Individual calculations are learned with a mentor.
questions.source: Lesson: The Laws of Family Purity (taharat ha-mishpachah)

questions.prompt: What do harchakot between spouses include during the days of niddah?
options: A ban on the wife lighting the Shabbat candles
No sleeping together, touching, or passing objects hand to hand
The husband's obligatory fast until the evening of the mikveh
A ban on any conversation for all seven days
questions.explanation: Harchakot are considerate distances: the spouses do not sleep together, avoid touching, and avoid passing objects directly from hand to hand. This is a pause before G-d, not a punishment.
questions.source: Lesson: The Laws of Family Purity (taharat ha-mishpachah)

questions.prompt: Immersion in the mikveh takes place on the evening of the seventh clean day.
questions.explanation: If nothing new appeared during the seven clean days, on the evening of the seventh day the woman is purified by full immersion in the mikveh. The seven days are named in Vayikra 15:28.
questions.source: Lesson: The Laws of Family Purity (taharat ha-mishpachah)

differs.text: In Masorti the laws of family purity formally remain, but their observance, including the count of days and the mikveh, is left to the family's discretion.
The Reform movement does not consider the laws of niddah binding; the mikveh may be a voluntary spiritual choice.

questions.prompt: At the tevilah a woman immerses seven times in a row in front of the whole family.
questions.explanation: The woman immerses once, briefly, and in complete privacy. Only the mikveh attendant is present.
questions.source: Lesson: The Laws of Family Purity (taharat ha-mishpachah)

questions.prompt: Match each image of family purity with the lesson's explanation of it.
pairs: a spring or rain of the required measure
only she sees the immersion itself
this is how tradition compares the mikveh
purity was broader than one bedroom
questions.explanation: The mikveh gathers living water of the required measure. The attendant sees the immersion, the mikveh is compared to the womb, and the tractates of Tahorot show that the system of purity was broader than the family.
questions.source: Lesson: The Laws of Family Purity (taharat ha-mishpachah)

questions.prompt: What is the immersion of new dishes in the mikveh called?
questions.explanation: The lesson calls the mikveh broader than marriage: with it giyur is completed, new dishes are immersed — tevilat keilim — and personal spiritual milestones are marked.
questions.source: Lesson: The Laws of Family Purity (taharat ha-mishpachah)

questions.prompt: On the eve of the chuppah the bride goes to the mikveh. Why is this needed, and how does this evening open the family's married life?
questions.modelAnswer: Before the wedding I understand the bride's immersion as the beginning of the rhythm of the whole of family life. From this evening the cycle of niddah, clean days, and the mikveh becomes constant. In Orthodox halacha this is a mitzvah of the Torah and the Oral Law. The pause and the later reunion renew closeness: separation is respect for holiness, not a punishment. We will go over the details of the count with a mentor.
keyPoints: The bride immerses on the eve of the wedding
From this evening the cycle becomes the family's rhythm
In Orthodoxy these laws are binding
The meaning of the cycle is pause and renewed reunion
questions.explanation: The lesson says that the bride immerses before the wedding and that from this evening the cycle becomes the family's rhythm.
questions.source: Lesson: The Laws of Family Purity (taharat ha-mishpachah)

differs.text: In Masorti the mikveh before the wedding is encouraged as a spiritual practice, but is not considered a required condition of piety.
In Reform communities immersion before the chuppah may be a voluntary symbol; the laws of niddah are not binding.

questions.prompt: Where besides married life did tradition know tumah and taharah, and what of this remained after the Temple?
questions.modelAnswer: I understand that tumah and taharah were broader than our bedroom: washings before service in the Temple, rules after childbirth, and other cases. The tractates Tahorot, Niddah, and Mikvaot deal with these. After the destruction of the Temple, the living, everyday part remained in the family, and holiness passed into the home. For me the mikveh is broader than marriage: with it giyur is completed, new dishes are immersed, and one prepares for a festival. I accept this as a holiness that the couple keeps on their own.
keyPoints: The Temple, childbirth, and the tractates Taharot, Niddah, and Mikvaot
After the Temple, the daily home practice remained
The mikveh also for giyur, dishes, and personal milestones
questions.explanation: The lesson shows that family purity is the surviving part of the great system of tumah and taharah after the destruction of the Temple.
questions.source: Lesson: The Laws of Family Purity (taharat ha-mishpachah)

questions.prompt: Who writes the divorce document according to the rules?
options: Any relative of the husband who can read
The wife herself, if the court allows it
A specially trained scribe — a sofer
A witness who only signs
questions.explanation: A get is written by a sofer — a specially trained scribe — according to exact rules and with two witnesses. An error in the text can invalidate the document.

questions.prompt: Which formula forms the core meaning of the get?
options: “Behold, you are consecrated to me with this ring”
“May His great name be exalted and sanctified”
“May he come to Torah, to the chuppah, and to good deeds”
“Behold, you are permitted to any man”
questions.explanation: The core meaning of the get is “Behold, you are permitted to any man.” With the handing over of the scroll, the woman is free to remarry.

questions.prompt: In what case does the Torah place the obligation of yibbum on the brother of the deceased?
options: If a man died leaving no children
If the widow has already received a get before witnesses
If the deceased left sons and daughters
If the brother himself requests the rite on the day of the funeral
questions.explanation: If a man dies childless, the Torah speaks of yibbum: the brother marries the widow so that the name of the deceased does not disappear. Today, in traditional communities, chalitzah is obligatory instead.

differs.text: The Reform movement has abolished yibbum and chalitzah; in its communities this question does not arise.

questions.prompt: What does the Lieberman clause, with which Masorti supplements the ketubah, obligate in advance?
options: It forbids the wife ever to ask for a divorce
To submit to the decision of a beit din if the marriage breaks down
It permits a kohen to marry a divorcee
It replaces the get scroll with a civil certificate
questions.explanation: Since 1953, the Conservative movement, through the Lieberman clause, obligates the spouses in advance to submit to a beit din if the marriage breaks down, so that the get cannot be withheld for extortion.
questions.source: Lesson: Divorce: the get and the agunah

questions.prompt: A mistake in a name, date, or word does not invalidate a get.
questions.explanation: A mistake in names, dates, or words can invalidate a get. That is why only trained scribes write it, and one does not begin without an experienced beit din.
questions.source: Lesson: Divorce: the get and the agunah

questions.prompt: After a get, a divorcee becomes forbidden to a kohen in marriage.
questions.explanation: The lesson recalls the verse: a kohen does not marry a divorcee. After a get, the woman is free to remarry, but she is forbidden to a kohen.

questions.prompt: Match the rule of divorce with its content.
pairs: this is how the scroll is handed over before two witnesses
only then does the beit din intervene
Does not provide for her and humiliates her
the wife may ask for a divorce through the court
A mamzer is not at fault
the weight of the status, not the person's guilt
questions.explanation: The handing over of the get — from hand to hand before two witnesses — must be voluntary. The wife may demand a divorce if the husband does not provide for her or humiliates her, and the mamzer himself is guilty of nothing.

questions.prompt: What does the Torah call the divorce document?
questions.explanation: In Devarim 24:1 the divorce document is called sefer keritut — a “scroll of severance”: it is written and placed into the wife's hand.

questions.prompt: You live in the diaspora, and a marriage will have to be ended. How does the handing over of a get differ from the decision of the state, and why might a Reform rabbi still advise the scroll?
questions.modelAnswer: For me in the diaspora, civil law and Jewish law run side by side: the state processes its own divorce, while a marriage according to the Torah ends with the handing over of a get. Until the husband has placed the scroll into the wife's hand, she remains his wife according to halacha. Since the nineteenth century, the Reform movement has considered a civil divorce sufficient, and the get is not required there. Many Reform rabbis still advise completing it, so as not to create halachic difficulties for the children in a traditional community. I find out in advance how my community decides, and I will not withhold the document out of spite.
keyPoints: In the diaspora, the two procedures run in parallel
According to halacha, the marriage ends with the handing over of the get
In Reform, a civil divorce is sufficient
A get is often advised for the sake of future children
questions.explanation: The lesson separates the civil divorce from the get and notes that many Reform rabbis advise a get for the sake of the children.

differs.text: In Reform Judaism a civil divorce is sufficient; the get is not required; many rabbis nonetheless advise completing a get so as not to create halachic difficulties for the children.

questions.prompt: Who performs the taharah and dresses the deceased in tachrichim?
options: Only the family's eldest son
The rabbi, who then recites the kaddish
Volunteers of the hevra kaddisha
Neighbors bringing the first meal
questions.explanation: The hevra kaddisha is a holy society of volunteers: they wash the body, dress it in simple white tachrichim, and prepare it for burial.

questions.prompt: What is the period before the funeral called, when the relatives are occupied only with the burial?
options: Shloshim
Yahrzeit
Yizkor
Aninut
questions.explanation: Aninut is the time before the funeral: the closest relatives are occupied only with arranging the burial. Then shiva begins.

questions.prompt: What is placed on the grave instead of flowers?
options: A small stone and good deeds in place of the deceased
A large floral wreath from the community
A burning candle on the wooden cover
A white ribbon over the burial shrouds
questions.explanation: Flowers are not brought to the cemetery. Memory is expressed simply: a small stone on the grave and good deeds in place of the deceased.

questions.prompt: The kaddish is composed in Aramaic, and it contains no words about death.
questions.explanation: The kaddish is an Aramaic hymn exalting G-d and His kingdom. There is not a word about death in it; it is recited by those who mourn.

questions.prompt: A funeral may be postponed for the convenience of distant acquaintances.
questions.explanation: The ideal is to bury on the day of death or the next day. A delay is permitted for the sake of Shabbat and the festivals, the arrival of close relatives, or the requirements of the law.

questions.prompt: Match the farewell custom with its meaning.
pairs: the washing of the body before burial
the tearing of the garments of the relatives at the funeral
words of repentance at the deathbed
there the kaddish is recited during the first week
questions.explanation: The body is washed, the relatives tear their garments, the vidui is recited with the departing one when needed, and during the first week the kaddish is heard in the house of mourning.

questions.prompt: What is the meal of consolation called after returning from the cemetery?
questions.explanation: The first meal after the cemetery is the seudat a-avra'a, the meal of consolation: it is brought by neighbors, not prepared by the grieving family itself.

questions.prompt: Why is the first yahrzeit treated with special care? Rely on the words of the Sages.
questions.modelAnswer: I remember the words of the Sages: the departed does not leave the hearts of the loved ones until twelve months have passed. That is why I keep the first yahrzeit with special care, as Moed Katan 27b teaches. On that day I light a candle for twenty-four hours, say kaddish, I may come to the grave, and I take on additional Torah study. The same period is the year of mourning for parents, without public celebrations and entertainments. For me, this is a continuation of love.
keyPoints: Moed Katan 27b: the heart does not let go before a year
Hence the care for the first yahrzeit
Candle, kaddish, grave, Torah study
A year for parents without public celebrations
questions.explanation: The lesson connects the tenderness of the first yahrzeit with the words of the Sages: memory does not let go before twelve months.

questions.prompt: With what words of Iyov will you meet the death of a loved one, and what, according to the lesson, remains after a person?
questions.modelAnswer: I will meet death simply, without pathos. The words of Iyov will become mine: naked I came, and naked I shall return; G-d gave, and G-d has taken away, blessed be the name of G-d. Kohelet adds: the dust returns to the earth, and the spirit returns to G-d who gave it. Death does not erase a person: the soul lives on, and the memory of the righteous is a blessing. After me, I want to leave a good name and good deeds.
keyPoints: Iyov 1:21: G-d gave and G-d took away
Kohelet 12:7: dust to the earth, spirit to G-d
What remains is a good name and good deeds
questions.explanation: The lesson meets death with the words of Iyov and Kohelet and says that after a person remain a good name and good deeds.

questions.prompt: How does Reform Judaism relate to the mikveh today, if the laws of niddah are not considered binding?
options: The mikveh is often being revived as a spiritual source of transition: giyur, a wedding, personal milestones — by voluntary choice
The mikveh is forbidden in Reform communities
The mikveh is needed only for immersing dishes and nothing else
Every Reform woman is obligated to immerse monthly, as in Orthodox halacha
questions.explanation: There is no obligation of niddah, but the mikveh lives on as a rite of transition and personal holiness.
